strengths: Addresses genuine theoretical problem: removes T₁ → ∞ requirement of prior work with elegant logarithmic dependence on dimension and data properties
Strong technical contribution: Theorem 4.1 provides clean Wasserstein convergence bounds under realistic assumptions, removing problematic conditions from Kwon et al. [20]
Skillful technical execution: careful use of log-Sobolev inequalities (Lemma B.3), transport-entropy inequalities, and novel confinement region argument (Theorem 4.2)
Improved discretization complexity: O(1/ε² log(1/ε)) for Langevin phase vs. O(1/ε⁴) in prior DDPM analysis
Minimal assumptions: works with norm-subgaussian data and standard L² score loss (what practitioners minimize)
Well-written: clear algorithm description, good intuition for technical proof strategy, helpful discussion of parameter roles
weaknesses: Severely limited experiments: only three 2D toy datasets shown; no realistic benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CelebA, etc.), no high-dimensional experiments, no comparison with practical DDPM implementations

Incomplete discretization analysis: Proposition 6.1 requires additional regularity assumptions; analysis of reverse ODE discretization (4.2) deferred to future work; full end-to-end complexity not established

Unclear practical utility: no evidence theoretical advantages translate to real performance gains; practical values of T₁ and computational costs unknown; large constants (172, 256, 550) with unclear tightness
Restrictive technical conditions: MGF loss requirement b(T₁) ≤ 1/(550β)·ε²/(2+36βδ²) is tight; small δ < 0.054 required for discrete case; implicit conditions on estimator sequences add complexity
Limited scope: analysis restricted to Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process; extensions to variance-exploding and other common SDEs not analyzed despite practical importance
Technical mechanisms somewhat opaque: truncation operation (4.5) requires a priori knowledge of confinement region for ∇log p_{T₁}; verification in practice unclear

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis with sound mathematical framework and detailed proofs
Meaningful theoretical contribution: removes T₁ → ∞ requirement that caused divergence in [20] with fixed score error
General applicability with minimal assumptions (norm-subgaussian distributions, no bounded support requirement)
Weaker technical assumptions than prior work (removes lim_{t→∞} L_s(t) = -1 requirement)
Mild logarithmic dependence on dimension and subgaussian norm in the lower bound for T₁
weaknesses: The finite T₁ benefit is substantially overstated: convergence requires T₂ → ∞, replacing one infinite-time limit with another; no evidence of computational advantage
Severe theory-practice gap: continuous-time theory only; discretization of reverse process (4.2) left for future work; main theorems inapplicable to practical discrete implementations

ε_MGF loss is stronger than L² loss minimized in practice; Theorem 4.2 fixes this via truncation requiring knowledge of ∇log p_T₁ and complex parameter constraints (b(T₁) ≤ 1/(550β)e^{2+36βδ²}) that are opaque for practitioners
Minimal empirical validation: only three toy 2D experiments (Gaussian mixture, two moons, swiss roll); no real datasets, no comparison with baselines, no computational time analysis
Limited algorithmic novelty: predictor-corrector scheme is from [33]; the contribution is merely running Langevin at time T₁ before reverse ODE, not a methodological advance

Technical assumptions hard to verify in practice: Assumption (A1) requires controlling one-sided Lipschitz constant L_s(t) with no practical algorithm; the additional technical assumption after Theorem 4.1 is vague
No practical guidance provided: paper offers no systematic method for selecting δ, τ, T₁, T₂ on real data; parameter interdependencies are complex but not well analyzed
Figure 1 omits truncation required by Theorem 4.2, creating a mismatch between theory and experiments; no ablation studies on the truncation's practical necessity

strengths: Addresses a genuine theoretical limitation: removes T₁ → ∞ requirement from prior convergence analysis (e.g., [20]) by showing T₁ need only depend logarithmically on dimension and data properties, not on final precision
Rigorous theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 provides W₂ convergence without unrealistic assumptions; removes requirement that lim_{t→∞} L_s(t) = -1; depends only on L² loss minimized in practice
Novel technical approach: clever truncation argument (Theorem 4.2) to bound stronger ϵ_MGF loss using confinement region reasoning and exploit fast convergence to stationary distribution
Improved discrete complexity: Proposition 6.1 shows O(1/ε² log 1/ε) steps versus O(1/ε⁴) in prior work [8,10], matching optimal Langevin algorithm rates for LSI distributions
Minimal assumptions: only requires norm-subgaussian data (covers practical cases) and qualitative Lipschitz continuity; does not need pointwise score control
Comprehensive treatment: includes discretization analysis, full proofs in appendix, three-term error decomposition is transparent, proof strategy well-motivated
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only synthetic 2D datasets (Figure 1); no experiments on images, audio, or realistic data; no comparison with standard methods; Figure 1 merely plots W₂(p,p_θ) vs T₂ without ablations or baselines

Gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.2 requires score truncation (claimed 'purely technical' but adds overhead); non-standard lim sup condition on L_s integral lacks practical guidance; large constants (172, 16, etc.) in T₁ bounds unexplained

Incomplete discretization results: Section 6 leaves open 'rigorous convergence guarantees for discretizations of (4.2)'; Proposition 6.1 requires extra smoothness assumptions (L₁-Lipschitz ∇log p_{T₁})
Limited practical guidance: trade-off parameter δ ∈ (0,1) is opaque; how to choose T₁, T₂ in practice?; early stopping time τ requires prior regularity knowledge; no computational cost analysis
Restricted scope: analysis limited to Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (extensibility claimed but unproven); only continuous time fully developed

Technical concerns: confinement region argument (Appendix C) feels somewhat ad-hoc; dependence on recent [7] for log-Sobolev bounds adds technical machinery; factor I_τ(T₁) = exp(T₁ - τ + ∫L_s) could be large in practice

strengths: Addresses a genuine theoretical problem: prior convergence bounds require T₁ → ∞ yet suffer from divergence for fixed score approximation error, creating a tension that this paper resolves
Non-trivial key insight: using log-Sobolev inequalities of p_{T₁} to enable fixed finite T₁ via fast inexact Langevin convergence; the application of recent results [8] is creative
Technically sound proofs with well-structured analysis: clear pipeline of bounding reverse process → Langevin dynamics → combining via log-Sobolev regularization
Theoretically improves upon prior work [24]: removes T₁ → ∞ requirement and one-sided Lipschitz assumption on score estimator at infinity
Mild logarithmic dimension dependence and minimal data assumptions (norm-subgaussianity) are favorable
Comprehensive treatment: extends beyond continuous ODE analysis to discretized schemes (Theorem 5.1) and other variants; honest discussion of concurrent work [11]
Clever technical innovation (Theorem 4.2): truncation scheme connecting standard L² loss to stronger MGF loss via confinement region
Practical loss control: requires only L² loss minimized in practice, not uniform pointwise bounds
Well-organized presentation with helpful intuition (e.g., confinement region Figure 2, clear proof sketches)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: algorithm is a straightforward variant of predictor-corrector scheme from [39]; main contribution is theoretical analysis of an existing approach
Implicit parameter dependence partially offsets fixed T₁ claim: T₁ still grows logarithmically with ‖X‖_{SG} and dimension; authors acknowledge ‖X‖_{SG} 'may still depend on d'

Stronger loss requirements introduce complexity: main theorem requires controlling ε_{MGF} (stronger than L² loss by factor 1/(1-δ)); while addressed via Theorem 4.2, this adds technical overhead and requires specific T₁ scaling
Bounds involve many parameters and constants: free parameters (δ, T₂, τ) require tuning; constants like 172, 24L₁L₂ appear without clear interpretation; complexity may limit practical utility
Minimal practical validation: Figure 1 shows only toy 2D examples; no wall-clock time comparisons, empirical verification of T₁ scaling, or validation that ε_{MGF} is small in practice
Missing comparisons with contemporary work: no quantitative comparison of sample complexity with [9, 12, 26]; no justification for two-stage vs. alternating correctors [11]
Technical condition in Footnote 3 (lim sup of integral) appears necessary but is not motivated upfront; not immediately clear why this assumption is natural
Unclear practical impact: two-stage algorithm adds complexity; convergence rate is qualitatively similar to existing methods; no empirical demonstration of benefits
Heavy technical notation and complex parameter relationships (I_τ(t), early stopping region τ ∈ [0, min{T₁, d/(2‖X‖²_{SG})}]) that could be more transparent
Norm-subgaussianity assumption (A2), while covering most practical cases, is still restrictive compared to general subgaussian; justification could be stronger

strengths: Addresses genuine theoretical limitation: Removes T₁ → ∞ requirement from prior work, which is conceptually important for understanding convergence trade-offs
Rigorous technical analysis: Careful proofs using modern tools (log-Sobolev inequalities, optimal transport); clean error decomposition into three components
Practical alignment: Bounds depend only on L² loss minimized in practice; Theorem 4.2 cleverly converts L² control to ε_MGF via truncation/confinement
Comprehensive theory: Covers both continuous-time (Wasserstein) and discrete-time (total variation) convergence with implementable algorithms
Clear exposition of key ideas: Section 4.1 proof sketches and Figure 2 effectively convey intuition about log-Sobolev regularization
weaknesses: Severe lack of experimental validation: Only 3 toy 2D datasets; no comparisons with standard methods [24, 25] or concurrent work [11]; no large-scale experiments; missing details on architecture and hyperparameters

Unclear practical advantage of fixed T₁: The bound still has explicit dimension dependence (T₁ ∝ log d); T₂ must be large for Langevin convergence; total computation time includes both T₁ and T₂; no empirical evidence of speedup over baselines

Loose bounds with multiple error terms: √3τd early-stopping error can be large in moderate d; integrated L² loss term involves exponential factors I_τ(T₁); ε_MGF term adds overhead; no empirical investigation of how tight bounds are

Restrictive assumptions: Norm-subgaussian (A2) excludes heavy-tailed data; integrated L² loss control (equation 4.4) requires uniform score approximation quality across [τ, T₁], which may be impractical

Limited novelty: Removes one assumption from [24] but replaces with another (ε_MGF); Langevin correction idea mentioned in [19]; uses existing results [8, 46]; discretization analysis in Section 5 follows standard approaches [9, 12]
Many dimension dependencies obscure claims: T₁ ≥ ½log(2 + 172∥X∥²_SG/δ + d/2δ); early stopping error √3τd; constants (172, 1/550) appear conservative and are not justified as tight

No head-to-head bound comparison: No table comparing rates/constants across [24, 25, 12] under matched assumptions; no computational complexity analysis vs. standard methods; unclear when this method is preferable

strengths: Addresses a genuine theoretical gap: Removes the T₁ → ∞ requirement from prior work, enabling fixed finite-time forward processes with convergence guarantees
Comprehensive and rigorous technical analysis combining log-Sobolev inequalities, optimal transport, and clever confinement arguments with complete proofs
Practical relevance: Minimal assumptions (norm-subgaussian, Lipschitz score), control via L² loss that's actually minimized in practice, extends to both continuous and discretized settings
Well-presented theoretical results: Clear main theorems, good intuitive explanations via proof sketches, extensive related work discussion, and solid mathematical exposition

Novel technical contributions: The confinement region argument (Lemma C.2) for controlling the stronger ϵ_MGF loss and the integration of recent results on Gaussian convolutions [8] are technically creative
weaknesses: Trade-off with prior work not fully resolved: While removing T₁ → ∞, introduces ϵ_MGF requirement with condition (4.7) requiring very small L² error at T₁ (factor 1/550), creating a different but substantial assumption

Severely limited experimental validation: Only toy 2D datasets (Gaussian mixture, two moons, Swiss roll); no comparison with standard methods, no real image generation, no ablation studies, no wall-clock time comparisons

Unclear practical impact: Fixed T₁ advantage is primarily theoretical; it's unclear if learning score for [0,T₁] is easier than [0,T_large], no evidence the algorithm improves actual sampling speed or sample quality
Opaque constants and conditions: T₁ dependence involves arbitrary-seeming constants (172, 1/550); unclear if bounds are tight or just artifacts of proof technique

Quantitative dependence on one-sided Lipschitz constant: While claimed 'qualitative,' the term I_τ(t) = exp(t−τ+∫L_s(r)dr) enters quantitatively and can explode if L_s is large, with limited guidance on controlling it
Incremental over concurrent work: Papers [11, 26, 4] study similar questions with different techniques; the unique algorithmic novelty is limited, primarily analytical
Discretization analysis requires stronger assumptions: Theorem 5.1 needs Lipschitzness of both ∇log p_t and s_θ(T₁,·), beyond Assumption (A1)
